title: Vishvamitra, the seer who saw the Gayatri
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a king becomes a sage among sages, and who the who is
carry: the rishis saw the verse; the god stirs minds
tomorrow: the verse has one word left, and it asks for something. what?

lines: HE SAID HE'D BRING IT. WHICH HE?
cards: Half the confusion in any group chat is pronouns. He said he'd bring it. Which he?
The Gayatri has the same knot in its second line: dhiyo yo nah. Yo means who. So who is the who: the radiance, or the god?
The answer is the god. And the man who first heard the verse never claimed to be it.

teach.h: YAH IS MASCULINE: IT MEANS THE GOD.
teach.b: Here's how a reader knows. Yah, who, is masculine. The radiance is neuter.
So who points to the god, Savitr. Dhiyo: thoughts, many of them. Nah: our.
Who, our thoughts. Now finish the week's story. After he left his throne, Vishvamitra's austerities kept breaking.
Once it was anger: in the Ramayana, he curses a nymph sent to distract him, feels his power drain away, and vows never to be angry again.
Years later, at the end of a long fast, a stranger begs for his food, and he gives it all away without a word.
Then the gods hail him as a brahmarshi, a sage among sages, and he asks for one more voice. Vasishtha, the sage whose staff had beaten him, says it too, and the old rivals become friends.
Tradition remembers him as the seer of the Gayatri. Seer is the right word.
Hindus call the Vedas shruti, what was heard: the rishis didn't invent the mantras, they saw them and heard them.

teach.h: THE SEER SAW. THE GOD STIRS.
teach.b: So even the verse's own seer isn't its who. The who is the god, asked to stir our thoughts. The week, end to end: a king's lesson and two verbs.
Tat, pointing to Brahman. Savitr's sun at sandhya. Varenyam, the good chosen.
The radiance nobody owns. Dhimahi, always we. And who, our thoughts.

how: In some families the Gayatri is given at the sacred-thread ceremony and said at home each day; others teach it openly to anyone. Its invocation names Vishvamitra as its rishi, the seer who saw it. Teachers who explain it word by word show that yah, who, points to Savitr.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a sage who wrote the Vedas from his own ideas
a king who became a sage among sages, and the god who stirs our thoughts
a king who defeated Vasishtha in battle

games.q: the last knot — tap the pairs.

s: yo, who, points back to the radiance
the radiance is neuter and yah is masculine: who is the god, Savitr.
Hindus hold that the rishis saw or heard the Vedic mantras rather than inventing them
that's why the Vedas are called shruti, what was heard.
Vishvamitra became a brahmarshi by finally beating Vasishtha
he gave up anger and gave away his food; then Vasishtha greeted him as one.

games.q: a classmate says 'Vishvamitra wrote the Gayatri.' what would many Hindu teachers say?
o: yes, he wrote it as a king's anthem.
he saw it: the Vedas are shruti, heard by the rishis, not invented.
nobody connects him with it at all.
games.why: tradition names him the Gayatri's seer, its rishi. and the verse itself points past him: the who is the god, asked to stir our thoughts.

practice: Listen for one sound that keeps going on its own: a fan, traffic, a fridge, rain. Let it be the only thing you follow. When a thought pulls you off, notice it, one of the many, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece, lightly: dhiyo yo nah, who, our thoughts, and the who is the god, not the seer.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dhiyo yo nah, who, our thoughts.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the rishis saw the verse; the god stirs minds, ours included. A week, done.
